title: How Do We Deal with Anxiety about the Internet?
text_original: right away, but engage your kids in occasional conversations about how things are going online as well as offline. See what they know about cyberbullying, ask if they know others who have experienced it, if it’s a problem at their school and what they would do if they were cyberbullied or knew about others who were. If they seem obsessed about checking text messages and social apps, it could be because they’re worried about what’s being said about them. It may not be bullying, but it may be a sign your child needs a little extra support. The federal government’s StopBullying.gov website suggests that parents be on the lookout for signs such as difficulty sleeping, frequent nightmares, declining grades, not wanting to go to school, feelings of helplessness or decreased self-esteem. 4. What do I do if my child is cyberbullied? Cyberbullying cases are as individual as the people involved. So the general advice that’s all over the Web – not to react or retaliate, block the “bully,” and print out and keep evidence in case it’ll be needed – can help in some cases. But the most important thing to do is talk with your kids about what’s going on, help them think through what happened, how they feel about it, and what they’re going to do about it. text_simplified: Talk to your children constantly about the internet and the real world, and ask them about their experiences with cyberbullying. If children are overly concerned with WhatsApp messages and social media apps, this may be due to anxiety about what is being said about them.
